units.title: Exploration as data collection: epsilon, entropy and optimism
outcomes: Explain exploration as a data-collection choice and contrast directed optimism with undirected epsilon-greedy and entropy noise.
State the UCB selection rule and the regret criterion, and predict when epsilon-greedy suffers linear regret.
Name what an exploration bonus adds to a value target and what has to be tuned about it.
units.why: Every deep RL update eats data the current policy collected. If collection never visits the good regions, no update rule can recover them.

next.note: Turn the optimism bonus into count, pseudocount and prediction-error rewards.
Test exploration where rewards are sparse and comparisons are easy to rig.

study.title: Berkeley CS 285 Lecture 19: the exploration problem and optimistic deep RL
study.locator: Lecture 19, Part 1: the exploration problem with Montezuma's Revenge and the exploitation-versus-exploration definitions; Part 2: optimistic exploration in deep RL with the UCB exploration bonus and bonus-weight tuning

focus: Regret is cumulative opportunity loss written through gaps and visit counts, so minimizing regret and maximizing reward are the same objective stated two ways.
UCB picks \(\operatorname{argmax}_a Q_t(a) + c \sqrt{\ln t / N_t(a)}\): the second term is uncertainty, not noise, and it shrinks as \(N_t(a)\) grows.
Epsilon-greedy explores indiscriminately while optimism prefers actions that are nearly greedy or highly uncertain; that is why fixed \(\epsilon\) can keep paying linear regret.
In deep RL the bonus is added to the reward or value target, which makes the bonus weight a tuning parameter that changes the learned policy.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write regret as total opportunity loss and the UCB rule with all symbols defined. For \(Q = [0.9, 0.8]\), \(N = [100, 2]\), \(t = 102\) and \(c = 1\), compute UCB values 1.115 and 2.321 and pick arm 2 despite its lower mean, then explain why epsilon-greedy with fixed \(\epsilon > 0\) keeps linear regret.
traps: Reading UCB as mean plus noise. The bonus is a deterministic function of \(t\) and \(N_t(a)\); the randomness sits in the estimated means.
Assuming more exploration is always safer. A fixed bonus weight can drown the task reward, so the weight is part of the comparison, not a free setting.
Judging exploration by one training curve. Regret and coverage statements need counts and seeds, not a single run that happened to stumble onto reward.

selfTest.q: Two arms have means 0.9 and 0.8 with counts 100 and 2 after 102 pulls and c = 1. Which arm does UCB pick and why?
selfTest.a: Arm 2. Its UCB is about 2.321 against about 1.115 for arm 1, so uncertainty outweighs the lower mean.

selfTest.q: Why can epsilon-greedy with fixed epsilon have linear regret while UCB has sublinear regret?
selfTest.a: Fixed epsilon keeps pulling suboptimal arms a constant fraction of the time, so regret grows with t. UCB shrinks exploration of an arm as its count grows, so suboptimal pulls grow sublinearly.

selfTest.q: What does the bonus weight control when a UCB-style bonus is added to a deep RL target?
selfTest.a: How much the update prefers uncertain states over high-value states. Too large and the agent chases novelty instead of the task; too small and the bonus changes nothing.

selfTest.q: An agent scores highly once after random play. Does that show its exploration method works?
selfTest.a: No. One lucky trajectory shows reachability, not a method. Compare visit counts, success rates and regret across seeds under matched budgets.

units.stopWhen: You compute the UCB pick by hand, explain the linear-regret case for fixed epsilon, and state what a bonus weight changes in a deep RL target.

fit.note: CS234 Lectures 9 to 10 cover bandits, regret and UCB at explain depth and Berkeley Lecture 19 carries the deep RL bonus framing; no search needed.

units.title: Counts, pseudocounts, curiosity and intrinsic rewards versus shaping
outcomes: Explain counts, pseudocounts and prediction-error novelty, and when each bonus stays informative.
Derive the total-reward mix of extrinsic and intrinsic reward and show how beta changes the objective.
Implement a tabular count bonus and an RND-style predictor error on a small task without counting the bonus as task reward.
units.why: Sparse tasks give no gradient until the first success. Intrinsic rewards manufacture a signal from novelty, but the same signal can trap the agent in front of noise.

next.note: Measure intrinsic bonuses where rewards are sparse and shaping can mislead.
Plug exploration bonuses into off-policy actor-critic targets.

study.title: Pseudocounts from a density model
study.locator: arXiv:1606.01868v2 Sections 2 to 3: density model over states, learning-positive Definition 1, prediction gain and Theorem 1 relating pseudocounts to information gain, and the bonus built on the pseudocount form

study.title: Hands-on Modern RL 12.1: ICM and RND concepts
study.locator: Sections 1 to 3.1: sparse-reward motivation with total rewardmix, ICM state-prediction error with inverse and forward models, RND target and predictor with its intrinsic reward, and the ICM versus RND comparison (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Concepts only. The UCB line on this page drops the square root, so use the CS234 form with the root. Treat the 10-18 Montezuma probability and the Atari score claims as unverified author reports, not targets.

focus: Total reward is \(r^{total}_t = r^{ext}_t + \beta r^{int}_t\): with extrinsic 0, intrinsic 0.4 and \(\beta = 0.1\), the update sees 0.04, and changing \(\beta\) changes the optimum.
A usable bonus is computable from visited data and exhaustible: visited states must decay toward zero bonus or the agent farms novelty forever.
Pseudocounts generalize tabular counts through a density model, while RND skips densities and uses error against a frozen random target.
RND trains two value heads because extrinsic and intrinsic returns have different horizons: episodic task return versus non-episodic novelty return.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the total-reward mix, the ICM reward as half squared feature-prediction error, and the RND reward as squared predictor-minus-target error. Compute the 0.04 example above and explain the noisy-TV failure: ICM error never decays on unpredictable noise while the RND target has bounded complexity.
traps: Counting the bonus as task performance. Success rates and task returns must use extrinsic reward only; the bonus is training signal.
Trusting novelty from a representation without checking it. A bonus depends on features or densities, so a new encoder can flip which states look novel.
Treating episodic and non-episodic novelty as interchangeable. Non-episodic intrinsic return lets novelty leak across episode boundaries; RND Section 2.3 keeps two heads for exactly this reason.

selfTest.q: Extrinsic reward is 0, intrinsic reward is 0.4 and beta is 0.1. What update signal does the agent see, and what happens as beta grows?
selfTest.a: It sees 0.04. Larger beta pushes the policy toward novelty and away from the task optimum; the bonus weight is part of the objective.

selfTest.q: Why does ICM get stuck on a noisy TV while RND is more robust?
selfTest.a: ICM rewards forward-model error, which stays high on unpredictable noise. RND rewards error against a fixed finite-complexity target, so the error is bounded and decays with visits.

selfTest.q: Why does RND fit two value heads instead of one mixed return?
selfTest.a: Extrinsic return is episodic and intrinsic return is non-episodic with its own scale and horizon. One head would mix incompatible targets; two heads keep each bootstrap correct.

selfTest.q: A density model assigns high likelihood to a new state. What does its pseudocount say?
selfTest.a: High pseudocount, hence low bonus. The state looks familiar to the model whether or not a tabular count ever saw it, which is exactly the representation dependence to check.

units.stopWhen: You compute the mixed-reward example by hand, derive when each bonus decays, and keep bonus and task reward in separate columns of your results.

fit.note: Berkeley Lecture 19 plus the RND and pseudocount papers cover derivation depth and the hands-on page supplies concept examples; no search needed.

units.title: Sparse, delayed and deceptive rewards, success coverage and unfair comparisons
outcomes: Distinguish sparse, delayed and deceptive rewards and predict which one misleads a shaped-reward fix.
Measure state-action visitation and success coverage with an explicit distance or threshold rule.
Spot unfair exploration comparisons that hide extra interactions, privileged state or tuned bonuses.
units.why: Hard tasks punish the wrong measurement. An agent can improve reward while never covering the goal, and a comparison can favor the method that secretly saw more.

next.note: Lock the matched budgets that make exploration comparisons fair.
Summarize sparse-task runs with robust aggregates instead of lucky seeds.

study.title: HER: sparse binary rewards and the shaped-reward failure
study.locator: arXiv:1707.01495v3 Sections 4.2 to 4.4 with Figures 3 to 5: DDPG with and without HER on pushing, sliding and pick-and-place over 5 seeds with the 7 cm and 20 cm success rule, and the failure of every shaped reward tried

study.title: CS234 Lecture 12: PAC, MBIE-EB and generalization
study.locator: Lecture 12: PAC framework for MDPs, MBIE-EB with its exploration bonus, and the generalization slides where raw counts fail when each state appears once and bonus terms are computed at visit time

focus: HER uses binary sparse reward \(r = -[\lvert g - s \rvert > \epsilon]\): 0 on success and -1 elsewhere, with success defined by an explicit distance such as 7 cm for pushing.
Deceptive means the shaped signal points away from the goal: HER Section 4.4 shows shaped rewards failing everywhere while sparse plus relabeling succeeds.
Coverage is measured over visited states and achieved goals, not over reward collected; a high-reward run can still cover almost nothing.
Fair comparisons match interactions, updates, information access and tuning: HER reports 5 seeds with standard-deviation bands and tunes its count-based baseline over a stated grid.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the HER binary reward and the pushing success rule, then sketch a visitation table for a small grid that separates success rate from state coverage. Explain in two sentences why the shaped rewards in HER Section 4.4 failed: they optimize distance while success is a threshold, and they penalize the touching behavior exploration needs.
traps: Replacing coverage with return. An agent can raise return by exploiting a nearby reward while the goal region stays unvisited.
Accepting a tuned baseline at face value. HER footnote 6 tunes its count baseline over alpha and beta grids; an untuned baseline comparison proves nothing.
Calling a task sparse when it is deceptive. Sparse needs more visits; deceptive needs a different signal, and extra visits to the wrong region make things worse.

selfTest.q: An agent doubles its episode return but visits the same 5 percent of states. Has exploration improved?
selfTest.a: Not shown. Return measures exploitation of visited regions; exploration needs visitation or success-coverage numbers over the state or goal space.

selfTest.q: Why did shaped distance rewards fail on the HER manipulation tasks while sparse binary rewards with HER succeeded?
selfTest.a: The shaped rewards optimize distance while success is a radius threshold, and they penalize imprecise touching, which teaches the agent not to touch the box. Sparse reward plus relabeling keeps the true objective and densifies signal honestly.

selfTest.q: Method A beats method B but used twice the environment steps and a tuned bonus. What do you demand before accepting the win?
selfTest.a: A rematch with matched steps, updates, information access and tuning budgets, plus per-run records and coverage numbers, not just mean return.

selfTest.q: Each state appears once in a large task. Why do raw counts stop helping?
selfTest.a: Every count stays near zero so every bonus looks the same. Novelty then needs generalization through densities, features or predictor error, with the representation dependence stated.

units.stopWhen: You report visitation and thresholded success separately from return, and you can reject an exploration win that hides extra steps, state or tuning.

fit.note: HER supplies sparse-task evidence with a success rule, hands-on supplies the bonus requirements, and CS234 Lecture 12 covers counts failure; no search needed.
